query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy coating on a Cu matrix, whose overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation behavior across different temperatures remain unclear, what single intervention could improve its wear resistance under sliding conditions spanning different temperatures, friction velocities, and wear depths? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to the unchanged FeNiCrCoCu coating tested under identical conditions, defines the operating limits of the prediction, cites supporting evidence from the introduction, and proposes a falsification experiment capable of resolving microscopic deformation during wear.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of titanium to the FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy coating can improve its wear resistance under sliding conditions spanning different temperatures, friction velocities, and wear depths.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy coating on a Cu matrix
generation.conditions: Sliding conditions with varying temperatures, friction velocities, and wear depths
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a protective oxide layer and/or cubic phases
generation.mechanism: The addition of titanium can increase the hardness, strength, and wear resistance of the alloy, potentially leading to the formation of a protective oxide layer and/or cubic phases that enhance wear resistance
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved wear resistance compared to the unchanged FeNiCrCoCu coating tested under identical conditions
generation.baseline: Wear resistance of the unchanged FeNiCrCoCu coating
generation.boundary: Temperature range: room temperature to elevated temperatures; friction velocities: low to high; wear depths: shallow to deep
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism by which titanium improves wear resistance is unclear, and further research is needed to fully understand the effects of titanium addition on the microstructure and properties of the FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy coating

falsification_experiment.design: Sliding wear tests with varying temperatures, friction velocities, and wear depths
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of titanium does not result in improved wear resistance compared to the unchanged FeNiCrCoCu coating, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 . Keywords: high-entropy alloy (HEA), compositionally complex alloy (CCA), spark plasma sin

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) present a new approach of alloying concepts. Whereas conventional alloys usually comprise one major alloying element and minor additions of other alloying elements to improve properties, HEAs consist of at least five elements with close to equimolar composition. For several compositions, the desired formation of solely solid solutions with a face-centred cubic (fcc) or a body-centred cubic (bcc) structure could be achieved [ [1] , [2] , [3] ].

Several groups of HEAs have been intensively investigated. The term compositionally complex alloys (CCAs) was introduced for HEAs with a multiphase microstructure [ [4] ]. Several investigations prove the formation of primarily cubic phases in the alloy AlCoCrCuFeNi and its derivatives [ [5] , [6] , [7] ]. Aluminium strongly influences the microstructure, phase formation and resulting properties. Furthermore, aluminium acts as a stabiliser of bcc solid solutions and can suppress the formation of complex phases [ [8] , [9] , [10] ].
